The ultimate wet weight for adult females, representing the maximum body mass attained by the species, is documented at 406 grams [Wwi = 406 grams], although field surveys and museum records indicate a broader range of 178 to 435 grams, reflecting substantial geographic and individual variation linked to prey abundance and latitude. This interval between fledging and reproductive activation allows young birds to hone their hunting skills and accumulate the necessary fat reserves to survive the winter.

The annual reproductive frequency for this species is notably high, with up to 15 nesting attempts possible each year [F_R_i = up to 15 nesting attempts possible each year], a strategy that permits a rapid numerical response to transient peaks in rodent abundance, a classic example of an irruptive predator adapting its output to fluctuating prey resources.

Adult survival in the wild, assessed under core body temperature conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reveals a maximum lifespan of approximately 7,957 days [am = approximately 7,957 days], which translates to nearly 22 years. This considerable longevity is an outlier among similarly sized strigids and is thought to be facilitated by the species' nomadic lifestyle, which allows individuals to track resource pulses across vast landscapes and avoid the density-dependent mortality associated with localized population crashes. The combination of high annual fecundity and an extended reproductive window means that even modest survival rates among adults can sustain populations through the lean years of low prey abundance. The physiological demands of such a long life are considerable, requiring efficient metabolic function and the robust storage of energy reserves to endure periods of food scarcity, particularly during harsh winter conditions in the northern parts of the range.

This prodigious capacity positions the Short-eared Owl as one of the most fecund of the strigids, a life-history trait that has evolved in concert with the boom-and-bust cycles of its primary prey, the microtine rodents. Comparative studies with other open-country owls, such as the Northern Harrier, indicate that this high reproductive ceiling is a convergent adaptation to unstable food resources, emphasizing the central role of trophic ecology in shaping avian life-history strategies.
